group.title: Core grammar
group.blurb: Pronouns, the present tense, the two verbs you cannot avoid, and how to show who owns what. Everything else in Dutch sits on top of these four.

topics.title: Subject pronouns
topics.summary: Nine subject pronouns, each with a strong and a weak form, plus when u is worth the effort and why zij is ambiguous.

rows: always lower case unless it starts the sentence

blocks.body: `jij / zij / wij` are the **stressed** forms and `je / ze / we` the **unstressed** ones. In normal speech the weak form is the default. Reach for the strong form only when you are contrasting people.

items.en: And you? Where do YOU live?

items.nl: Wij gaan naar Frankrijk, zij gaan naar Spanje.
items.en: We are going to France, they are going to Spain.

blocks.title: Overusing the strong form
blocks.body: Saying `jij` and `wij` in every sentence makes you sound insistent, as if you were always correcting someone. If you are not contrasting, use `je` and `we`.

`u` is the polite you. It covers **one person or several**, and it always takes a **-t** on the verb: `u woont`, `u bent`, `u hebt`.
- Use `u` with older people, officials, doctors, and anyone at a counter.
- Use `je` with colleagues, classmates, shop staff your own age, and anybody who says `je` to you first.
- If in doubt, start with `u`. Dutch people will often invite you down with `Je mag je zeggen, hoor.`

items.nl: Mevrouw Jansen, hebt u een minuutje voor mij?
items.en: Mrs Jansen, do you have a minute for me?

items.nl: Meneer, weet u hoe laat het is?
items.en: Sir, do you know what time it is?

blocks.title: zij can be she or they
blocks.body:
The **verb** tells you which one:
- `Zij is de beste moeder.` (she is)
- `Zij zijn 1 en 3 jaar oud.` (they are)
If the sentence is still ambiguous, use a name or `ze allebei` to clear it up.

blocks.title: jullie is not formal
blocks.body: `jullie` is simply the plural of `je`. It is informal. To address a group politely, use `u`: `Wilt u allemaal gaan zitten?`

blocks.title: het does more than it
blocks.body:
`het` stands in for a het-word (`Waar is het boek? Het ligt daar.`), and it also carries weather, time and general statements where English uses "it":
- `Het regent.`
- `Het is drie uur.`
- `Het is koud vandaag.`

blocks.title: je as a general you
blocks.body: Like English "you", `je` can mean people in general: `In Nederland fiets je overal naartoe.` (In the Netherlands you cycle everywhere.) Nobody specific is meant.

key_takeaways: Use the weak forms je, ze, we by default and the strong forms jij, zij, wij only for contrast.
u is polite, works for one person or many, and always takes -t on the verb.
zij is both she and they, and only the verb tells them apart.
jullie is plural and informal, so it is not the polite option.

exercises.prompt: De docent heet Jan. ___ werkt maandag en woensdag.
exercises.explain: Jan is one man, so hij.

exercises.prompt: Ik en mijn vriend hebben een relatie. ___ wonen samen sinds een jaar.
exercises.explain: Ik plus another person gives wij or we. The verb wonen confirms a plural subject.

exercises.prompt: Dit zijn mijn honden. ___ zijn 1 en 3 jaar oud.
exercises.explain: Two dogs, so the plural zij or ze. The verb zijn shows it is plural, not singular.

exercises.prompt: The teacher asks the whole class: Begrijpen ___ de grammatica?
exercises.explain: A group being addressed informally takes jullie.

exercises.prompt: You are at the doctor's desk. Which is right?
exercises.explain: A stranger in an official setting takes u, and u takes the -t form hebt (heeft is also accepted).

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses the strong form correctly?
options: Jij woont in Utrecht en jij werkt daar.
Wij gaan naar Frankrijk, zij gaan naar Spanje.
exercises.explain: The strong forms earn their place when two groups are being contrasted.

exercises.prompt: Het regent. What is het doing here?
options: referring to a het-word mentioned earlier
carrying the weather, like English it
exercises.explain: het carries weather, time and general statements: Het regent, Het is drie uur.

topics.title: The present tense
topics.summary: Find the stem, add nothing, add -t, or use the base form. Three endings cover every regular Dutch verb, and one rule about jij explains most mistakes.

blocks.body:
Take the base form (the dictionary form, called the `infinitief`), cut off `-en`, then fix the spelling with the two sound rules:
- **wonen** minus -en gives wo-, and the o must stay long, so double it: stem `woon`
- **zitten** minus -en gives zitt-, and one t keeps the i short: stem `zit`
- **reizen** minus -en gives reiz-, but no word ends in z: stem `reis`
- **blijven** minus -en gives blijv-, but no word ends in v: stem `blijf`

blocks.note: Notice the plural row is simply the base form again. That is three quarters of the work done.

blocks.title: The four spelling patterns side by side
blocks.note: zit does not become zitt, because Dutch never writes a double t at the end of a word.

sections.heading: The jij rule: drop the t after the verb

blocks.body:
When `jij` or `je` comes **directly after** the verb, the `-t` disappears. This happens in questions and after any inversion.
- `Jij woont in Utrecht.` gives `Woon je in Utrecht?`
- `Jij bent docent.` gives `Ben je docent?`
- `Jij kookt pasta.` gives `Kook je pasta?`
- `Morgen werk je thuis.` (inversion, so no -t)

blocks.title: Only jij and je
blocks.body: The t stays with everybody else: `Woont u in Utrecht?`, `Woont hij in Utrecht?`, `Wonen jullie in Utrecht?`. The rule is about the word `jij/je`, not about questions in general.

sections.heading: Stems that already end in t or d

blocks.body:
Dutch never writes `tt` or `dt` at the end of a word, but it does write `dt` in the middle of a form.
- `heten` has stem `heet`, so `jij heet` (adding a t would give heett, which is not allowed)
- `sporten` has stem `sport`, so `zij sport`
- `worden` has stem `word`, so `jij wordt` and `hij wordt` (d plus t is written out)
- `vinden` has stem `vind`, so `hij vindt`

blocks.title: wordt versus word
blocks.body: `ik word` (stem only) but `jij wordt` and `hij wordt` (stem plus t). In a question with je the t drops again: `word je moe?`. This is the classic mistake Dutch people make too.

blocks.note: komen looks irregular but is not: ko-men has a long o that would need doubling, yet the stem is kom with a short o. Learn it as an exception.

sections.heading: What the Dutch present tense covers

blocks.body:
One Dutch present tense does the work of several English ones. There is no separate "am doing" form.
- `Ik werk.` = I work **and** I am working.
- `Ik woon hier al twee jaar.` = I have been living here for two years.
- `Ik ga morgen naar Utrecht.` = I am going to Utrecht tomorrow (near future).

blocks.title: If you really need to stress right now
blocks.body: Use `aan het` plus the base form: `Ik ben aan het koken.` (I am cooking right now.) Save it for when the timing genuinely matters.

key_takeaways: Stem for ik, stem plus t for jij, u, hij, zij, het, and the base form for all plurals.
After the verb, jij and je knock the -t off: woon je, ben je, kook je.
A stem ending in t gets no second t (jij heet), a stem ending in d does (jij wordt).
One present tense covers I work, I am working, and I am going tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form: Jij ___ in Badhoevedorp. (wonen)
exercises.explain: jij takes stem plus t, and the stem of wonen is woon.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form: De meisjes ___ altijd naar werk. (fietsen)
exercises.explain: A plural subject takes the base form: fietsen.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form: Karolina ___ twee keer per week. (sporten)
exercises.explain: The stem sport already ends in t, so no second t is added.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form: ___ jij ook Engels? (spreken)
exercises.explain: jij follows the verb, so the -t drops: Spreek jij ook Engels?

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form: Peter ___ nooit zijn huiswerk. (maken)
exercises.explain: Stem maak (long a doubled) plus t for hij.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form: Hij ___ een brief aan zijn vrouw. (schrijven)
exercises.explain: Stem schrijf (v becomes f at the end) plus t.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
exercises.explain: jij right after the verb removes the -t.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
exercises.explain: The t only drops for jij and je. u keeps it: Woont u?

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
exercises.explain: The stem is word, and jij adds a t, so wordt. Only ik word has no t.

exercises.prompt: Build: I walk to my work because it is nearby.
exercises.explain: want joins two main clauses and does not change the word order after it.

topics.title: hebben and zijn
topics.summary: The two most common Dutch verbs, both irregular, both needed in almost every sentence. Plus the fixed expressions that decide which one you need.

blocks.title: In questions with je the t drops here too
blocks.body:
- `Jij hebt tijd.` gives `Heb je tijd?`
- `Jij bent moe.` gives `Ben je moe?`
And as always, `u` keeps its form: `Hebt u tijd?`, `Bent u moe?`

blocks.title: u hebt or u heeft
blocks.body: Both are correct and both are common. `u hebt` follows the pattern more strictly, `u heeft` sounds a touch more formal. Pick one and stay consistent.

rows: Ik ben moe. Hij is blij.
Ik ben te laat. Jij bent nooit op tijd.
Mijn broer heeft een afspraak bij de tandarts.
Ik heb honger. Wij hebben dorst.
Ik heb last van mijn rug.

blocks.title: The two that flip compared to English
blocks.body:
- Age takes **zijn**: `Ik ben 37`, never `ik heb 37 jaar`.
- Hunger and thirst take **hebben**: `Ik heb honger`, never `ik ben hongerig` in normal speech.
These two catch nearly every learner in the first month.

items.note: a state, so zijn plus op tijd

blocks.body:
English "there is / there are" is `er is / er zijn`, and the verb agrees with what follows.
- `Er is een café op de hoek.`
- `Er zijn twee cafés in de straat.`
In a question the order flips: `Is er een toilet hier?`

key_takeaways: hebben: heb, hebt, heeft, hebben. zijn: ben, bent, is, zijn.
In a question with je both drop the t: heb je, ben je. With u they do not: hebt u, bent u.
Age, profession, nationality and states take zijn.
Hunger, time, appointments, being right and possession take hebben.

exercises.prompt: Ik ___ twee broers en drie zussen. En jij?
exercises.explain: Possession takes hebben, and the ik-form is heb.

exercises.prompt: Mijn kat ___ heel blij met zijn nieuwe huisje.
exercises.after: heel blij met zijn nieuwe huisje.
exercises.explain: blij is a state, so zijn. Third person singular gives is.

exercises.prompt: Mevrouw Jansen, ___ u een minuutje voor mij?
exercises.explain: Possession of a minute takes hebben, and u accepts both hebt and heeft.

exercises.prompt: ___ jij morgen in de les?
exercises.explain: Location takes zijn, and jij after the verb removes the t: Ben jij?

exercises.prompt: Mijn broer ___ morgen een afspraak met de tandarts.
exercises.after: morgen een afspraak met de tandarts.
exercises.explain: An appointment is something you have, so heeft for hij.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'You are never on time'?
exercises.explain: op tijd zijn is being punctual. tijd hebben is having free time.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Ik ben hongerig van het eten.
exercises.explain: Hunger is something you have in Dutch: Ik heb honger. Age, by contrast, uses zijn.

exercises.prompt: Build the question: are you tired? (informal)
exercises.explain: Verb first in a yes/no question, and bent loses its t before je.

exercises.prompt: Complete: ___ een toilet hier?
exercises.explain: One toilet is singular, and in a question the verb comes first: Is er een toilet hier?

topics.title: Possessive pronouns
topics.summary: My, your, his, her, our, their. Only one of them changes shape, but that one (ons or onze) catches everybody.

blocks.body:
This is the only possessive that changes, and the rule is short:
- `ons` before a **singular het-word**: `ons huis`, `ons appartement`, `ons kind`
- `onze` **everywhere else**: `onze buren`, `onze auto`, `onze moeder`, `onze kinderen`
If you do not know whether a word is a de-word or a het-word, `onze` is the safer bet, because it covers three of the four cases.

items.nl: Ons appartement is precies naast hun appartement.
items.en: Our flat is right next to their flat.

items.nl: Onze buren heten Daan en Saïda.
items.en: Our neighbours are called Daan and Saïda.

blocks.body:
Same logic as the subject pronouns: `jouw` is the stressed form, `je` the everyday one.
- `Wat is je naam?` (neutral)
- `Dat is mijn fiets. Waar is jouw fiets?` (contrast)
Be careful with the spelling: `jouw` with a w is the possessive, `jou` without a w is the object form (`Dit is voor jou.`).

Dutch prefers `van` where English uses an apostrophe s.
- `de auto van mijn broer` = my brother's car
- `de zus van je moeder` = your mother's sister
- `de man van je oma` = your grandmother's husband
This is also how you build family riddles: `Wie is de zoon van je tante?`

blocks.title: When Dutch does use -s
blocks.body:
Names and close family words can take a plain `-s`, with no apostrophe:
- `Peters fiets`, `Esthers moeder`, `mijn moeders lievelingseten`
An apostrophe appears only when the name ends in a single long vowel letter (a, i, o, u, y) that the plain -s would spoil: `Anna's fiets`, `Rico's auto`, `Harry's tas`. A name ending in -e keeps the plain -s: `Sophies tas`.

blocks.title: zijn means his, not my
blocks.body:
Learners copy the possessive from the wrong person. Read this and spot the errors:
- Wrong: `Mijn naam is Sophie. Ik woon in Amsterdam met zijn vriend.`
- Right: `Mijn naam is Sophie. Ik woon in Amsterdam met mijn vriend.`
The possessive follows the **owner**, so if Sophie is speaking about her own boyfriend it is `mijn`.

blocks.title: zijn is also a verb
blocks.body: `zijn` is both the possessive "his" and the verb "to be". Word order tells them apart: after a subject it is the verb (`Ze zijn allebei 30 jaar`), before a noun it is the possessive (`zijn naam is Robert`).

key_takeaways: ons goes before a singular het-word, onze everywhere else.
jouw is the stressed form, je the everyday one, and jou without w is the object form.
Use van instead of an apostrophe s: de auto van mijn broer.
The possessive follows the owner, so a woman talking about her partner says mijn or haar, never zijn.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
exercises.explain: het appartement is a singular het-word, so it takes ons.

exercises.prompt: Complete with our: ___ buren heten Daan en Saïda.
exercises.explain: buren is plural, so onze.

exercises.prompt: Sophie is speaking about her own boyfriend. Fix the possessive: Ik woon in Amsterdam met ___ vriend.
exercises.explain: Sophie is the owner and the speaker, so mijn. zijn would mean his.

exercises.prompt: Which spelling means 'your name'?
exercises.explain: jouw with a w is the possessive. jou without a w is the object form, as in voor jou.

exercises.prompt: Build: my brother's car is new.
exercises.explain: Dutch builds possession with van: de auto van mijn broer.

exercises.prompt: Talking about Robert: ___ naam is Robert en hij is arts.
exercises.after: naam is Robert en hij is arts.
exercises.explain: Robert is male, so zijn (his).

exercises.prompt: The neighbours own the flat. Which is right?
exercises.explain: hun is the possessive for they.

exercises.prompt: Ask formally for someone's address.
exercises.explain: The formal possessive matching u is uw.

topics.title: The diminutive
topics.summary: Dutch adds a tiny ending to almost any noun to make it small, friendly or polite. Five endings, one sound rule to pick between them, and one article for all of them.

blocks.body:
The `verkleinwoord` (the little form) is not only about size. Dutch speakers reach for it constantly to sound warm, casual or polite.
- **small**: `het huisje` (the little house)
- **friendly**: `een biertje`, `een kopje koffie`
- **polite or brief**: `een momentje`, `een vraagje`
- **affectionate**: `het hondje`, `het neefje`

blocks.title: Two things are always true
blocks.body:
1. Every diminutive is a **het-word**, whatever the original was: `de stoel` becomes `het stoeltje`.
2. Every diminutive makes its plural with **-s**: `de huisjes`, `de kopjes`, `de biertjes`.
The ending is chosen by the **sound at the end of the word**, not by meaning. Work down this list and take the first rule that fits.

rows: huis, huisje / boek, boekje / kop, kopje
after a vowel, or after l, n, r, w following a long vowel
vrouw, vrouwtje / stoel, stoeltje / deur, deurtje / ei, eitje
after m following a long vowel or a consonant
boom, boompje / raam, raampje / arm, armpje
after a short vowel plus l, m, n, r or ng
bal, balletje / kam, kammetje / man, mannetje / ster, sterretje / ding, dingetje
blocks.note: The -etje group doubles the consonant, because the short vowel has to stay short. Same spelling rule as ik zit from zitten.

blocks.title: Words ending in a single vowel double it
blocks.body:
A word that ends in one vowel letter needs that vowel doubled before `-tje`, so the sound stays long:
- `auto` becomes `autootje`
- `paraplu` becomes `parapluutje`
- `cafe` becomes `cafeetje`
A word already ending in two vowels or a diphthong just takes `-tje`: `ei` becomes `eitje`.

sections.heading: Diminutives with a life of their own

blocks.body: Some diminutives have drifted away from their base word and are now the normal way to say the thing. You cannot use the big version instead.

rows: de meid, a maid or a girl, dated
het kwartier, the same but flatter
de kaart, the map or card

items.nl: Zullen we een kopje koffie drinken?
items.en: Shall we have a cup of coffee?

blocks.title: Do not overdo it
blocks.body: Sprinkled on food, drinks and requests, the diminutive sounds natural. Applied to serious things it sounds dismissive: `een probleempje` says the problem is not worth worrying about, which may not be what you mean.

key_takeaways: Every diminutive is a het-word and takes -s in the plural.
The ending follows the final sound: -je, -tje, -pje, -kje or -etje.
A short vowel plus l, m, n, r or ng takes -etje and doubles the consonant.
A word ending in one vowel doubles it first: auto becomes autootje.
Diminutives are as much about warmth and politeness as about size.

exercises.prompt: Which article goes with stoeltje?
exercises.explain: Every diminutive is a het-word, even though the base word is de stoel.

exercises.prompt: Make the diminutive of het boek.
exercises.explain: A plain consonant at the end takes -je: boekje.

exercises.prompt: Make the diminutive of de boom.
exercises.explain: An m after a long vowel takes -pje: boompje.

exercises.prompt: Make the diminutive of de man.
exercises.explain: A short vowel plus n takes -etje, and the n doubles to keep the vowel short.

exercises.prompt: Which is the diminutive of de auto?
exercises.explain: A word ending in one vowel doubles it before -tje: autootje.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of het kopje?
exercises.explain: Diminutives always take -s in the plural.

exercises.prompt: Why does a waiter say een biertje rather than een bier?
options: it sounds friendlier and more casual
exercises.explain: The diminutive is about tone as much as size. Drinks almost always take it in a café.

exercises.prompt: Ask politely for a moment of someone's time, using the little form.
exercises.explain: een momentje is softer than een moment, which is why it is the standard phrasing.
